title: As if it were the last
hookLine: do each act as if it were the last of your life, without pretense (Meditations 2.5)

lines: THE LAST WALK THROUGH THE HOUSE.
AS IF IT WERE THE LAST.
cards: Some last times announce themselves. The last day at a job. The last walk through an empty house before handing over the keys.
The last visit with a grandparent, when everyone quietly understood. On days like that, people tend to notice everything: the light, the creak in the floor, what gets said and how. Nothing is faked.
Marcus had just reminded himself that his time had a limit. His very next note says what to do about it. Today, as if it were the last.

teach.h: DO WHAT'S IN FRONT OF YOU.
teach.b: Meditations 2.5 is one long breath of a sentence.

teach.h: EVERY ACT AS IF THE LAST.
teach.b: Every moment, Marcus tells himself, do what's in front of you with simple dignity, with affection, with freedom and justice, and let every other thought go. How, with a mind that won't stop wandering?
His answer, in George Long's translation: "if thou doest every act of thy life as if it were the last."
And he lists what to leave behind: carelessness, resentment of what reason asks, self-love, discontent with your lot, and one that's easy to miss, hypocrisy. Pretending. Here's the heart of it.

When you know it's the last time, you stop performing. You don't answer your grandmother's question with half your attention while you check your phone. You don't make the last coffee at your old job with a sigh.
The last time makes you honest, and Marcus borrows that honesty for an ordinary Thursday. A fair worry: wouldn't that make you anxious? The Stoics would say no.

They didn't mean panic; they meant presence. The point isn't to feel doom while washing the dishes. It's to wash them with nothing held back and nothing faked, because this is the only washing you're actually doing.
The past one's gone, and the next one isn't here. The limit gave you the clock.
This gives you what to do while it ticks: one act at a time, whole and unpretending, as if the last.

how: Some readers of the Meditations use 2.5 as a guide for ordinary tasks, doing one thing at a time with full attention, and some modern Stoic practice pairs it with a morning reflection on the shortness of life.

games.q: your mind won't stop wandering, and you're trying to do the task in front of you well. what does Marcus tell himself?
o: do this act as if it were the last of your life.
games.why: "if thou doest every act of thy life as if it were the last." the last time makes you present and honest.

practice: Choose something small you can do right now: pour a glass of water, write one message, fold a shirt, look at someone you live with.
Do it slowly and completely, as if this were the last time you'd ever get to, with no hurry, no performing, nothing faked. Notice what you see that you usually miss.

wordCard.voice: Hypocrisy, the pretending Marcus told himself to leave behind when doing each act as if it were the last. Today's word.
